title: Sinusoids & RMS
description: Describe a sinusoid by its peak value, frequency and phase, and find its rms value and power.

study.title: Describing a sinusoid
study.body: We write every sinusoid as a **cosine**: $v(t) = V_m\cos(\omega t + \theta)$. $V_m$ is the **peak value** (amplitude): the waveform swings between $+V_m$ and $-V_m$, so the peak-to-peak value is $2V_m$. $\omega$ is the **angular frequency** in rad/s and $\theta$ the **phase angle**, usually given in degrees (mixed units: convert $\theta$ to radians before evaluating at a time $t$).

study.title: Frequency, period, angular frequency
study.body:
The **period** $T$ is the time of one cycle and the **frequency** $f = 1/T$ is the number of cycles per second (Hz). One cycle is $2\pi$ rad, so $\omega T = 2\pi$.
Example: 50 Hz mains has $T$ = 20 ms and $\omega = 2\pi\cdot 50 \approx 314$ rad/s.

study.title: Phase, lead and lag
study.body: Convert sines to cosines with $\sin(z) = \cos(z - 90^\circ)$, and remove a minus sign with $-\cos(z) = \cos(z \pm 180^\circ)$. For two sinusoids of the **same frequency** written this way, the one with the larger phase **leads**: it peaks earlier. $\cos(\omega t + 40^\circ)$ leads $\cos(\omega t + 10^\circ)$ by $30^\circ$. A phase difference $\Delta\theta$ is a time shift $\Delta t = (\Delta\theta/360^\circ)\,T$; for example, a negative $\theta$ moves the first peak to $t_{max} = (-\theta/360^\circ)\,T$.

study.title: Explore: amplitude, frequency and phase
study.body: Drag the sliders for $v(t) = V_m\cos(2\pi f t + \theta)$. $V_m$ stretches the wave vertically, $f$ squeezes it horizontally ($T = 1/f$). The grey dashed curve has $\theta = 0$: a **positive** $\theta$ shifts the wave to the **left** (it leads: its peaks come earlier), a negative one shifts it to the right (it lags). The first peak sits at $t = (-\theta/360^\circ)\,T$ for negative $\theta$.

study.title: RMS (effective) value
study.body: The rms value of a periodic voltage is the DC voltage that would deliver the same average power to a resistor: square, average over one period, take the square root. For a sinusoid it is $V_m/\sqrt2 \approx 0.707\,V_m$, independent of frequency and phase. Mains voltages are quoted as rms: 230 V rms has a peak of $230\sqrt2 \approx 325$ V.

study.title: Average power in a resistor
study.body: The instantaneous power $p(t) = v^2(t)/R$ pulses at twice the signal frequency between 0 and $V_m^2/R$. Its average uses rms values, exactly like the DC formulas. Using the peak value instead of the rms value is the classic mistake: it doubles the power.

steps.title: Peak, frequency, phase
steps.body: Every sinusoid is written as a **cosine**: $V_m$ is the **peak value** (the wave swings between $\pm V_m$), $\omega$ the **angular frequency** in rad/s and $\theta$ the **phase angle**, usually in degrees.

steps.prompt: Match each symbol to its meaning.
steps.explanation: In $v(t) = V_m\cos(\omega t + \theta)$: $V_m$ is the peak value, $\omega = 2\pi f$ the angular frequency, $f$ the number of cycles per second, $T = 1/f$ the duration of one cycle and $\theta$ the phase angle.

steps.title: Frequency and period
steps.body: One cycle takes the **period** $T$; the **frequency** $f = 1/T$ counts cycles per second (Hz). Since one cycle is $2\pi$ radians, $\omega T = 2\pi$, so $\omega = 2\pi f$. European mains: 50 Hz, $T$ = 20 ms, $\omega \approx 314$ rad/s.

steps.prompt: A sinusoid has frequency $f$ = {{f|Hz}}. Find its angular frequency $\omega$.
steps.explanation: $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi \times {{f}} = {{2*pi*f}}$ rad/s.

steps.prompt: For $v(t) = {{Vm}}\cos({{w}}t)$ V, what is the period $T$?
steps.explanation: $\omega$ = {{w}} rad/s, so $T = 2\pi/\omega = 2\pi/{{w}}$ = {{2*pi/w|s}}. (The frequency is $f = 1/T$ = {{w/(2*pi)|Hz}}.)

steps.title: Phase, sines and lead/lag
steps.body: Convert sines with $\sin(z) = \cos(z - 90^\circ)$: $10\sin(\omega t + 30^\circ) = 10\cos(\omega t - 60^\circ)$ has phase $-60^\circ$. For two sinusoids of the same frequency, the one with the larger phase angle **leads** (peaks earlier): $\cos(\omega t + 40^\circ)$ leads $\cos(\omega t + 10^\circ)$ by $30^\circ$.

steps.prompt: What is the phase angle $\theta$ of $v(t) = {{Vm}}\sin({{w}}t + {{ph}}^\circ)$ when written as ${{Vm}}\cos({{w}}t + \theta)$?
steps.explanation: $\sin(z) = \cos(z - 90^\circ)$, so ${{Vm}}\sin({{w}}t + {{ph}}^\circ) = {{Vm}}\cos({{w}}t + {{ph}}^\circ - 90^\circ)$ and $\theta = {{ph-90}}^\circ$. A sine lags the cosine of the same argument by $90^\circ$.

steps.prompt: $v_1(t) = 5\cos(\omega t + {{a}}^\circ)$ leads $v_2(t) = 5\cos(\omega t - {{b}}^\circ)$ by ${{a+b}}^\circ$.
steps.explanation: Both are cosines with the same frequency, so compare phases: $\theta_1 - \theta_2 = {{a}}^\circ - (-{{b}}^\circ) = {{a+b}}^\circ > 0$. So $v_1$ leads $v_2$ by ${{a+b}}^\circ$ (equivalently, $v_2$ lags $v_1$ by ${{a+b}}^\circ$).

steps.title: Try it: shifting the phase
steps.body: Drag $\theta$ and compare with the grey reference ($\theta = 0$). Increasing $\theta$ moves the wave **earlier** (to the left): it leads the reference. At $\theta = \pm 180^\circ$ the wave is simply inverted. Changing $f$ or $V_m$ does not change where, as a fraction of a period, the peaks sit.

steps.title: RMS value
steps.body: The **rms** (effective) value is the DC value that would deliver the same average power to a resistor. For a sinusoid it is the peak divided by $\sqrt2$. Mains voltages are quoted as rms: 230 V rms has a peak of $230\sqrt2 \approx 325$ V.

steps.prompt: Find the rms value of $v(t) = {{Vm}}\cos({{w}}t + {{th}}^\circ)$ V.
steps.explanation: $V_{rms} = V_m/\sqrt2 = {{Vm}}/\sqrt2$ = {{Vm/sqrt(2)|V}}. The frequency and phase do not affect the rms value of a sinusoid.

steps.prompt: $v(t) = {{Vm}}\cos({{w}}t - 30^\circ)$ V. Find the frequency $f$ in hertz.
steps.explanation: $f = \frac{\omega}{2\pi} = \frac{ {{w}} }{2\pi}$ = {{w/(2*pi)|Hz}}. Don't confuse $\omega$ (rad/s) with $f$ (Hz).

steps.prompt: A supply is rated {{V}} V rms. What is the peak value $V_m$ of its voltage?
steps.explanation: $V_m = \sqrt2\,V_{rms} = \sqrt2 \times {{V}}$ = {{V*sqrt(2)|V}}. Insulation and component voltage ratings must handle this peak, not just the rms value.

steps.prompt: The voltage $v(t) = {{Vm}}\cos(\omega t)$ V is applied to a {{R|Ω}} resistor. What is the average power absorbed?
steps.explanation: $P_{avg} = \frac{V_{rms}^2}{R} = \frac{V_m^2}{2R} = \frac{ {{Vm}}^2}{2\times {{R}} }$ = {{Vm^2/(2*R)|W}}. Using the peak value directly ($V_m^2/R$) doubles the answer.

steps.prompt: $v_1(t) = {{A}}\cos(\omega t + {{a}}^\circ)$ and $v_2(t) = {{B}}\sin(\omega t + {{b}}^\circ)$. By how many degrees does $v_1$ lead $v_2$? (Give a negative number if $v_1$ lags.)
steps.explanation: First write $v_2$ as a cosine: ${{B}}\sin(\omega t + {{b}}^\circ) = {{B}}\cos(\omega t + ({{b-90}}^\circ))$. Then $v_1$ leads $v_2$ by $\theta_1 - \theta_2 = {{a}}^\circ - ({{b-90}}^\circ) = {{a-b+90}}^\circ$. A negative result means $v_1$ lags. The amplitudes play no role.

steps.prompt: Two sinusoids of frequency {{f|Hz}} differ in phase by {{dth}}°. What time shift between their peaks does this correspond to?
steps.explanation: One period ($360^\circ$) lasts $T = 1/f$ = {{1/f|s}}. So $\Delta t = \frac{\Delta\theta}{360^\circ}\,T = \frac{ {{dth}} }{360}\times$ {{1/f|s}} = {{dth/360/f|s}}.

steps.prompt: A sinusoidal current delivers an average power of {{P|W}} to a {{R|Ω}} resistor. Find the **peak** value of the current.
steps.explanation: $P = I_{rms}^2 R$ gives $I_{rms} = \sqrt{P/R} = \sqrt{ {{P}}/{{R}} }$ = {{sqrt(P/R)|A}}. The peak is $I_m = \sqrt2\,I_{rms}$ = {{sqrt(2*P/R)|A}}.

steps.prompt: A {{V}} V DC source and a sinusoidal source with a {{V}} V **peak** value each drive identical resistors. Which resistor absorbs more average power?
options: The one on DC: twice as much
The one on AC: twice as much
The one on DC: √2 times as much
steps.explanation: The sinusoid has $V_{rms} = {{V}}/\sqrt2$ = {{V/sqrt(2)|V}}, and power is proportional to $V_{rms}^2$: $P_{AC}/P_{DC} = (1/\sqrt2)^2 = 1/2$. A DC voltage is its own rms value.

steps.prompt: $v(t) = 10\cos(\omega t - {{th}}^\circ)$ V with $f$ = {{f|Hz}}. At what time $t_{max} > 0$ does $v$ first reach its positive peak?
steps.explanation: The cosine peaks when its argument is zero: $\omega t - {{th}}^\circ = 0$. The peak is delayed by ${{th}}^\circ$ out of a $360^\circ$ cycle: $t_{max} = \frac{ {{th}} }{360}\,T = \frac{ {{th}} }{360}\times$ {{1/f|s}} = {{th/360/f|s}}.

steps.prompt: A sinusoid with period $T$ = {{T|s}} has its first positive peak after $t = 0$ at $t$ = {{k*T|s}}. Written as $V_m\cos(\omega t + \theta)$ with $-180^\circ < \theta \le 180^\circ$, what is $\theta$?
steps.explanation: At the peak the cosine argument is zero: $\omega t_1 + \theta = 0$, so $\theta = -\omega t_1 = -360^\circ\,\frac{t_1}{T} = -360^\circ\times {{k}} = {{-360*k}}^\circ$. A peak after $t = 0$ means the wave is delayed, i.e. a negative phase.

steps.prompt: Find the rms value of $v(t) = {{Vdc}} + {{Vm}}\cos(\omega t)$ V.
steps.hint: Square, average over one period, take the root.
steps.explanation:
$v^2 = V_{dc}^2 + 2V_{dc}V_m\cos\omega t + V_m^2\cos^2\omega t$. Over one period the middle term averages to 0 and $\cos^2$ averages to $\tfrac12$:
$$V_{rms} = \sqrt{V_{dc}^2 + \frac{V_m^2}{2}} = \sqrt{ {{Vdc}}^2 + \frac{ {{Vm}}^2}{2} } = {{sqrt(Vdc^2+Vm^2/2)}}\ \mathrm{V}$$
It is **not** ${{Vdc}} + {{Vm/sqrt(2)}}$: rms values of different components don't simply add.

steps.prompt: A current $i(t) = {{Im}}\sin(\omega t + 30^\circ)$ A flows through a {{R|Ω}} resistor. Find the average power absorbed.
steps.explanation: Sine or cosine and phase don't matter: $I_{rms} = {{Im}}/\sqrt2$ = {{Im/sqrt(2)|A}} and $P = I_{rms}^2R = \frac{I_m^2 R}{2} = \frac{ {{Im}}^2\times {{R}} }{2}$ = {{Im^2*R/2|W}}.

steps.prompt: A heater (a pure resistance) absorbs {{P|W}} from a {{V}} V rms supply. Find the **peak** current.
steps.explanation: For a resistor, voltage and current are in phase, so $P = V_{rms}I_{rms}$ and $I_{rms} = P/V_{rms} = {{P}}/{{V}}$ = {{P/V|A}}. The peak is $I_m = \sqrt2\,I_{rms}$ = {{sqrt(2)*P/V|A}}. (The heater resistance is $V_{rms}^2/P$ = {{V^2/P|Ω}}.)

steps.prompt: $v(t) = 50\cos(\omega t + {{tv}}^\circ)$ V and $i(t) = 2\cos(\omega t - {{ti}}^\circ)$ A. Which statement is correct?
steps.explanation: Phase difference: $\theta_v - \theta_i = {{tv}}^\circ - (-{{ti}}^\circ) = {{tv+ti}}^\circ$. It is positive, so $v$ leads $i$, i.e. $i$ lags $v$ by ${{tv+ti}}^\circ$. Subtracting the magnitudes of the angles (${{abs(tv-ti)}}^\circ$) ignores the minus sign.

steps.prompt: Doubling the frequency of a sinusoidal voltage across a resistor, keeping its peak value the same, changes the average power the resistor absorbs.
steps.explanation: For a resistor $P = V_m^2/(2R)$: no frequency appears. The rms value of a sinusoid depends only on its peak value. (For inductors and capacitors frequency does matter, as you'll see with impedance.)

steps.prompt: Write $v(t) = -{{Vm}}\cos(\omega t + {{th}}^\circ)$ as $V_m\cos(\omega t + \theta)$ with $V_m > 0$ and $-180^\circ < \theta \le 180^\circ$. What is $\theta$?
steps.explanation: A minus sign is a $180^\circ$ shift: $-\cos(z) = \cos(z \pm 180^\circ)$. To stay in range, subtract: $\theta = {{th}}^\circ - 180^\circ = {{th-180}}^\circ$, so $v(t) = {{Vm}}\cos(\omega t + ({{th-180}}^\circ))$.

steps.prompt: The graph shows a sinusoidal voltage $v(t)$.

ask.explanation: Measure one full cycle, e.g. from one positive peak to the next: $T$ = {{T|s}} (the graph shows two cycles). Then $f = 1/T$ = {{1/T|Hz}}.
One full cycle (peak to next peak) takes $T$ = {{T|s}}. Then $\omega = 2\pi/T$ = {{2*pi/T}} rad/s (that is $f$ = {{1/T|Hz}} times 2π).
The waveform swings between ±{{Vm|V}}, so the peak value is $V_m$ = {{Vm|V}} (half the peak-to-peak value). For a sinusoid $V_{rms} = V_m/\sqrt2$ = {{Vm/sqrt(2)|V}}.

steps.prompt: The graph shows $v_1(t)$ (solid) and $v_2(t)$ (dashed), two sinusoids of the same frequency. Which statement is correct?
steps.explanation: Compare two **positive** peaks that are less than half a period apart: the waveform that peaks **first** (further left) leads. Here they are $\Delta t$ = {{d/360*T|s}} apart and the period is $T$ = {{T|s}}, so the phase difference is $360^\circ\cdot\Delta t/T$ = {{d}}°. Comparing a positive peak of one with a negative peak of the other would give the wrong value 180° − {{d}}° = {{180-d}}°.

steps.prompt: The graph shows $v(t)$: a DC value plus a sinusoid. Find its rms value.
steps.hint: The DC part is the midline; the peak of the sinusoid is half the peak-to-peak swing.
steps.explanation: The midline (average) is $V_0$ = {{V0|V}}. The waveform swings from {{V0-Vm|V}} to {{V0+Vm|V}}, so the sinusoid has peak $V_m$ = {{Vm|V}}. A DC part and a sinusoid add **in power**: $V_{rms} = \sqrt{V_0^2 + V_m^2/2}$ = $\sqrt{{{V0^2}} + {{Vm^2/2}}}$ = {{ans|V}}. (Adding $V_0 + V_m/\sqrt2$ is wrong.)

steps.prompt: Which graph shows $v(t) = V_m\cos(\omega t - 90^\circ)$? Each graph shows one period starting at $t = 0$ (left axis).
steps.explanation: $\cos(\omega t - 90^\circ) = \sin\omega t$: it is 0 at $t = 0$ and rising, and reaches its positive peak a quarter period later. Subtracting 90° **delays** the cosine by $T/4$ (a lag). The cosine itself starts at its positive peak, $-\cos$ at its negative peak, and $-\sin$ = $\cos(\omega t + 90^\circ)$ falls first.

steps.prompt: The graph shows one period of $v(t) = V_m\cos(\omega t + \theta)$. Find $\theta$ in degrees ($-180^\circ < \theta \le 180^\circ$).
steps.hint: Find where the positive peak is. A cosine peaks where $\omega t + \theta = 0$.
steps.explanation: The positive peak is at $t_p$ = {{tp|s}}, i.e. {{tp/T}} of the period $T$ = {{T|s}}. A cosine peaks where $\omega t + \theta = 0$ (or a multiple of 360°), so $\theta = -360^\circ\cdot t_p/T$ = {{-360*tp/T}}°, which is the same angle as {{th}}°. Check: at $t = 0$, $v = V_m\cos\theta$ = {{round(100*Vm*cos(rad(th)))/100|V}}, and the curve is falling there if $\theta > 0$ (the peak has already passed) or rising if $\theta < 0$.

steps.prompt: Drag $\theta$ so that the plotted ${{Vm}}\cos(\omega t + \theta)$ V is the same waveform as $v(t) = {{Vm}}\sin(\omega t + {{phi}}^\circ)$ V ($f$ = 50 Hz).
steps.hint: A sine lags the cosine of the same argument by a quarter period.
steps.explanation:
Use $\sin(z) = \cos(z - 90^\circ)$:
${{Vm}}\sin(\omega t + {{phi}}^\circ) = {{Vm}}\cos(\omega t + {{phi}}^\circ - 90^\circ)$, so $\theta$ = **{{phi - 90}}°**.
Check on the graph: at $t = 0$ the waveform equals ${{Vm}}\sin({{phi}}^\circ)$ = {{Vm*sin(rad(phi))|V}}, and the first peak comes at $t = \frac{90^\circ - {{phi}}^\circ}{360^\circ}T$ if that is positive.
